source: Gibson and Birkinshaw (2002 working paper version of AMJ 2004) Contextual determinants of organisational ambidexterity
finding: Defines contextual ambidexterity as alignment plus adaptability inside one business unit. Context is built from four traits: stretch, discipline, support, trust. Authors say the traits are interdependent and not substitutable.
numbers: Hypothesis 1: more ambidexterity gives better performance. Hypothesis 2: the interaction of stretch, discipline, support and trust gives more ambidexterity.
limits: Theory part of the working draft. The AMJ 2004 version is the one usually cited.
agent_relevance: The agent could pair a strict check step (alignment) with a loose idea step (adaptability) inside one loop, not in two separate modules.

source: Gibson and Birkinshaw (2002 working paper version of AMJ 2004) Contextual determinants of organisational ambidexterity
finding: Sample design: survey of employees in 41 business units of ten multinational firms, aggregated to unit level. People who rated the cause (context) and people who rated the outcome (ambidexterity, performance) came from different management levels, to cut same-source bias.
numbers: 4234 survey respondents, 41 business units, 10 firms (the published AMJ abstract says 4,195 respondents). 50-500 employees surveyed per unit; interviews in 2-8 units per firm.
limits: Cross-sectional survey; perceived performance. Working-paper count 4234 differs from the published 4,195.
agent_relevance: Shows how to measure a two-sided trait without one rater: separate who rates the input from who rates the output.

source: Gibson and Birkinshaw (2002 working paper version of AMJ 2004) Contextual determinants of organisational ambidexterity
finding: Alignment and adaptability correlate positively across units. No unit scores low on both. K-means with 4 groups fit better than 3 groups (the 3-group version only gave low-low, mid-mid, high-high along the diagonal).
numbers: Alignment vs adaptability r = .50, p < .01 (n = 41). Four clusters: 7 Aligned, 11 Adaptive, 18 Moderately Ambidextrous, 5 Highly Ambidextrous.
limits: Clusters rest on small n. Authors warn units near cluster edges could switch group. The Aligned group is dominated by one firm.
agent_relevance: Treat the two abilities as separate axes, not one slider; the trade-off is weaker than balance theory implies.

source: Gibson and Birkinshaw (2002 working paper version of AMJ 2004) Contextual determinants of organisational ambidexterity
finding: Core result: ambidextrous groups perform best, aligned-only perform worst. Every pair of groups differs (post-hoc S-N-K).
numbers: Performance on a 7-point scale: Aligned 3.21, Adaptive 3.74, Moderately ambidextrous 4.10, Highly ambidextrous 4.60. ANOVA F = 18.11, p < .001.
limits: Performance is rated by the same kind of respondents who rate ambidexterity.
agent_relevance: Supports doing both fast adaptation and disciplined fit at once, but the evidence is correlational.

source: Gibson and Birkinshaw (2002 working paper version of AMJ 2004) Contextual determinants of organisational ambidexterity
finding: Robustness check with different raters (senior raters for performance, junior raters for alignment and adaptability) keeps the same group ranking, but the top two groups stop differing significantly.
numbers: Means 3.41 (Aligned), 3.88 (Adaptive), 4.11 (Moderately), 4.13 (Highly). F = 5.57, p < .01. Top two groups not significantly different.
limits: The headline gap between moderate and high ambidexterity is fragile once same-source bias is removed.
agent_relevance: Do not trust a claim that maximal balance beats moderate balance; the clean evidence only shows that both beat one-sided.

source: Gibson and Birkinshaw (2002 working paper version of AMJ 2004) Contextual determinants of organisational ambidexterity
finding: Second robustness check: adding the 4 nearest units to the Aligned group (to dilute a single-firm effect) keeps the pattern.
numbers: Means 3.42, 3.80, 4.14, 4.60. F = 13.59, p < .001; all four groups differ. Enlarged-group context tests gave F = 3.67, 3.53, 3.92.
limits: Same 41 units, so not independent data.
agent_relevance: The ordering holds; the size of the gap varies with the design.

source: Gibson and Birkinshaw (2002 working paper version of AMJ 2004) Contextual determinants of organisational ambidexterity
finding: Context predicts ambidexterity. Aligned-only units had the lowest performance-management and social context. The Adaptive group performs better than the Aligned group, hinting that adaptability matters more.
numbers: Social context correlates r = .52 with adaptability and r = .45 with performance; adaptability with performance r = .78; alignment with performance r = .54 (unit level, n = 41). Interaction term ANOVA F = 5.41, p = .003.
limits: Table text came out garbled in extraction, so the context group means are not recorded here; r and F values are as printed.
agent_relevance: Adaptability tracks outcome much more tightly (r .78) than alignment (r .54): flexibility is the bigger lever.

source: Gibson and Birkinshaw (2002 working paper version of AMJ 2004) Contextual determinants of organisational ambidexterity
finding: Interviews show several paths to ambidexterity (equifinality). A French auto engineering unit added adaptability on top of alignment; a US oil and gas unit used a loose-tight model; a US software consulting unit blended both. Low units suffered inertia.
numbers: Group 4 had five units: three from the French auto firm, one software consulting, one oil and gas.
quote: ability to turn on a dime
limits: Anecdotal, five top units only. Senior executives played a larger role than the authors expected (a top-down push was still needed).
agent_relevance: Matches a loose-tight scaffold: fixed outer rules, free inner search. Warns that someone senior must pick which new ideas get resources.

source: Gibson and Birkinshaw (2002 working paper version of AMJ 2004) Contextual determinants of organisational ambidexterity
finding: Validity check: subjective performance correlates with financial performance relative to industry peers.
numbers: r = .75 between subjective performance and 5-year ROA, ROE and shareholder return relative to peers (firm level).
limits: Firm level, not unit level; peer groups chosen by the authors.
agent_relevance: Rating-based measures can be partly validated against hard outcomes; worth doing for agent evals too.

source: Wikipedia (2026 snapshot) Organizational ambidexterity
finding: Summary of the field: structural (separate units), contextual (same unit) and temporal cycling. Duncan 1976 coined the term; March 1991 launched the research. Lists critics: ambidexterity may be unattainable, small firms may do better focused, very low levels of both give no gain.
numbers: He and Wong 2004: interaction positive for sales growth, imbalance negative. Atuahene-Gima 2005: exploitation negative for radical innovation, exploration positive. Chandrasekaran 2012: 34 high-tech organisations, simultaneous pursuit linked to higher performance.
limits: Secondary source; several claims uncited; most sample sizes missing. Orientation only.
agent_relevance: Background map; primary papers carry the numbers.

source: He and Wong (2004) Exploration vs exploitation: an empirical test of the ambidexterity hypothesis, Organization Science 15(4) 481-494
finding: Tests whether firms that balance exploration and exploitation do better. Two fit tests: the interaction of the two innovation strategies relates positively to sales growth; a relative imbalance between them relates negatively.
numbers: 206 manufacturing firms; outcome is sales growth rate. IDEAS lists 777 citations and 19 references (March 1991, Levinthal and March 1993, Burgelman 1991, Ghemawat and Costa 1993, Levinthal 1997 among them).
limits: I opened only the abstract and reference list, not the full text, so regression coefficients are not recorded. Sample country not confirmed from sources read.
agent_relevance: The two tests split ambidexterity into a combined and a balance idea; the agent can log both the amount of search and its ratio to refinement.

source: He and Wong (2004), via O'Reilly and Tushman (2007 HBS WP 07-088) summary
finding: O'Reilly and Tushman cite He and Wong and Venkatraman et al. 2006 as finding that ambidexterity goes with higher sales growth.
numbers: Sales growth link in both studies (no coefficients given in this source).
limits: Second-hand citation.
agent_relevance: Supports the direction of the claim, not its size.

source: Jansen, Van den Bosch, Volberda (2006) Exploratory innovation, exploitative innovation and performance (ERIM working paper version)
finding: Study of units in a European financial firm: how formal and informal coordination relate to exploratory and exploitative innovation. Two-wave design (antecedents in 2002, outcomes about ten months later, performance up to a year after).
numbers: Wave 1: 769 units in 220 branches sent survey; 462 returned (60 percent). Wave 2: 283 units in 115 branches, final response rate 36.8 percent. Mean unit size 33.37 full-time staff.
limits: One firm, one industry, one country. New scales for exploratory and exploitative innovation.
agent_relevance: Moderately large two-wave field data; a template for separating cause from outcome in time.

source: Jansen, Van den Bosch, Volberda (2006) Exploratory innovation, exploitative innovation and performance (ERIM working paper version)
finding: Centralisation hurts exploration; formalisation helps exploitation; connectedness helps both. Not every prediction held.
numbers: Centralisation to exploratory beta = -0.17 (p<.01); to exploitative beta = 0.04 (ns). Formalisation to exploratory beta = -0.07 (ns); to exploitative beta = 0.18 (p<.01). Connectedness to exploratory beta = 0.20 and to exploitative beta = 0.21 (both p<.01); inverted-U for connectedness not supported (squared term -0.08, ns).
limits: Hypotheses 1b, 2a and 3a failed. Standardised betas from a single-industry sample.
agent_relevance: Informal links (shared context) beat formal rules for supporting both modes, which mirrors contextual ambidexterity. Rules need not kill exploration if designed to enable.

source: Jansen, Van den Bosch, Volberda (2006) Exploratory innovation, exploitative innovation and performance (ERIM working paper version)
finding: Environment moderates payoff. Exploration pays in dynamic markets; exploitation pays in stable markets and in competitive markets.
numbers: Exploratory x dynamism beta = 0.15 (p<.01); exploitative x dynamism beta = -0.23 (p<.001); exploitative x competitiveness beta = 0.19 (p<.001); exploratory x competitiveness beta = -0.05 (ns, hypothesis not supported).
limits: The competitiveness result for exploration contradicted the prediction; authors suggest duration of rivalry as a reason. Financial performance followed for one year only.
agent_relevance: A strong boundary condition: how much the agent explores should depend on how fast the task environment changes, not be fixed.

source: Jansen, Van den Bosch, Volberda (2006) Exploratory innovation, exploitative innovation and performance (ERIM working paper version)
finding: Informal coordination predicts both innovation types better than formal coordination in model comparisons. Authors link connectedness to contextual ambidexterity.
numbers: Full model compared with models holding only formal (centralisation, formalisation) or only informal (connectedness) mechanisms; informal explains more for both types.
limits: Single-firm design; no effect sizes beyond the betas above.
agent_relevance: Suggests building shared context across agent sub-steps rather than adding more gating rules.

source: O'Reilly and Tushman (2007 HBS WP 07-088) Ambidexterity as a dynamic capability
finding: Distinguishes sequential (Duncan 1976) from simultaneous or structural (Tushman and O'Reilly 1996-97) ambidexterity. The simultaneous form needs separate subunits, each internally aligned, joined by shared strategic intent, common values, linking mechanisms and a senior team with common-fate incentives.
numbers: Literature review found more than 40 studies of ambidexterity, using case studies, simulations, formal models, lab and field work.
limits: Review by the proponents; favours the structural view.
agent_relevance: Gives a design list for a multi-part agent: separate explore and exploit roles plus one integrator with a shared goal.

source: O'Reilly and Tushman (2007 HBS WP 07-088) Ambidexterity as a dynamic capability
finding: Tushman et al. (cited) studied 22 innovation attempts in 13 companies. Ambidextrous designs beat functional, cross-functional and spin-out designs; the exception was product substitution, where simpler designs won.
numbers: 22 innovation attempts, 13 companies. Switching to an ambidextrous design linked to more innovation; existing-product performance also higher in ambidextrous firms.
limits: Reported second-hand from a working paper; few cases; authors are the theory's proponents.
agent_relevance: Structure choice depends on task type: spin off when the new thing replaces the old, integrate when it can use existing assets.

source: O'Reilly and Tushman (2007 HBS WP 07-088) Ambidexterity as a dynamic capability
finding: Counter-evidence is listed: Christensen says explorers must be spun out; strategy work says firms pursuing both get stuck in the middle; Ebben and Johnson found dual-strategy small firms did worse.
numbers: Ebben and Johnson 2005: 300 small companies; firms pursuing both efficiency and flexibility performed worse than focused firms. Van Looy et al. 2005 simulation: ambidextrous forms costly but sustainable and superior if well managed.
limits: Summaries only; I did not open the originals.
agent_relevance: Balance can be costly; a light-weight agent may do better focusing than balancing.

source: O'Reilly and Tushman (2007 HBS WP 07-088) Ambidexterity as a dynamic capability
finding: Antecedents: ambidexterity is more likely in dynamic environments (Jansen et al. 2005, Lee 2003, Raisch 2006) and with senior team behavioural integration (Lubatkin et al. 2006, 139 small businesses). A shared vision predicted ambidexterity in 211 banks (Jansen 2006).
numbers: Lubatkin: 139 small businesses; Jansen: 211 banks.
limits: Second-hand.
agent_relevance: A common goal text and a single integrator matter more than module count.

source: March (1991) Exploration and exploitation in organizational learning, as quoted in Gibson and Birkinshaw
finding: Core theoretical claim: pure exploration pays experimentation costs without benefits; pure exploitation traps a system in suboptimal stable equilibria; balance is a main factor in survival.
numbers: Only the March (1991, p71) quote was read, in the working paper. March's own model (mutual learning of organisational code and individuals; competition for primacy) was not opened.
quote: maintaining an appropriate balance between exploration and exploitation is a primary factor in system survival and prosperity
limits: Only the quote was read this session; the formal model was not opened (PDF host failed).
agent_relevance: The founding trade-off that the agent's explore-versus-refine control borrows from.

source: Cao, Gedajlovic, Zhang (2009) Unpacking organizational ambidexterity, Organization Science 20(4) 781-796
finding: Splits ambidexterity into a balance dimension (equal levels) and a combined dimension (total magnitude) with different mechanisms. Both high together give synergy. Balance helps resource-poor firms; combined magnitude helps resource-rich firms.
numbers: No sample numbers in the pages I read (abstract summary only; the Semantic Scholar TLDR agrees).
limits: Full text not opened (publisher blocked). Direction of effects from the abstract summary only.
agent_relevance: Budget matters: with tight compute, balance explore and refine; with spare compute, raise both.

source: Jansen et al. (2006) Management Science 52(11), abstract via IDEAS
finding: Independent summary of the same findings: centralisation lowers exploration, formalisation raises exploitation, connectedness raises both, exploration pays in dynamic settings, exploitation pays in competitive settings.
numbers: See the Jansen betas above.
limits: Abstract-level check only.
agent_relevance: Cross-check of the working-paper numbers against the published version's claims; direction matches.

source: Raisch and Birkinshaw (2008) Organizational ambidexterity: antecedents, outcomes, moderators, Journal of Management 34(3) 375-409
finding: Review that organises the field into antecedents, moderators and outcomes. Only the abstract was seen, via Semantic Scholar metadata.
numbers: Citation count 2842 (Semantic Scholar, Nov 2026).
limits: Full text was restricted; nothing beyond the abstract was read.
agent_relevance: Listed for completeness; read later if a deeper review is wanted.

source: Junni, Sarala, Taras, Tarba (2013) Organizational ambidexterity and performance: a meta-analysis, Academy of Management Perspectives 27(4)
finding: A meta-analysis of the ambidexterity-performance link exists (907 citations on Semantic Scholar). The publisher page returned 403 and no abstract was available, so I cannot report effect sizes.
numbers: Citation count only.
limits: Not opened. Do not quote effect sizes from this line. Needs a second pass.
agent_relevance: This is the key piece for the question of whether balance helps; it is a gap to fill.

source: Gupta, Smith, Shalley (2006) The interplay between exploration and exploitation, AMJ 49(4) 693-706
finding: Cited in the sources read as distinguishing sequential from simultaneous ambidexterity and noting that they pose different management challenges. Not opened.
numbers: 3421 citations (Semantic Scholar).
limits: Not opened.
agent_relevance: Background only.

source: Atobishi and Nosratabadi (2026) Dynamic capabilities for AI-enabled exploration
finding: Closest AI-related ambidexterity paper found. It is a survey of firms, not an LLM test, and says generative AI lowers the cost of the exploration side of ambidexterity. AI-enabled exploration drives innovation performance through a sensing-capability chain.
numbers: 245 valid responses from Saudi executives (600 invited, 268 returned, 40.8 percent effective rate), PLS-SEM. Sensing to AI-enabled exploration beta = 0.530; AI-enabled exploration to innovation performance beta = 0.604 (f2 = 0.576). Government support to sensing beta = 0.098, not significant. Gaussian copula terms non-significant; SME vs large multigroup showed no path differences.
limits: Self-reported survey, one country, cross-sectional. Table text in my extraction was garbled, so verify against the PDF. Preprint, not yet published.
agent_relevance: Not a test of an LLM agent; shows how people frame generative AI as an exploration tool inside firms.

source: Haider, Zubair, Saleem (2024) Big data analytics-enabled dynamic capabilities and market performance: marketing ambidexterity
finding: Survey of Pakistani textile retailers using PLS-SEM; reports a positive path from marketing ambidexterity (exploitation-oriented) to market performance. Not about LLMs.
numbers: One path in the results text: b = 0.242, t = 3.843, p = 0.000.
limits: Small convenience sample; the extracted text had unfinished fields (N = ?). Low quality evidence.
agent_relevance: Shows how loosely 'ambidexterity' is now used in AI-adjacent work; little value for our design.

source: arXiv title search for ambidexterity and LLM agents (Nov 2026)
finding: Searching arXiv for 'ambidexterity' returned 22 results. Most are mathematics (homotopy theory) or robotics. No paper tests organisational ambidexterity on LLM agents. A broader keyword search was too noisy to use.
numbers: 22 results for 'ambidexterity'; only 1 is about AI in firms (2607.02645); 3 others are IT or big-data survey studies.
limits: Covers arXiv only and one query term; other venues and wording (exploration-exploitation in multi-agent systems) were not covered. Semantic Scholar, OpenAlex and the arXiv API were rate limited during this run.
agent_relevance: Honest gap: no direct LLM test of structural vs contextual ambidexterity was found. Another angle should look under exploration-exploitation in LLM agents.

source: Semantic Scholar citation metadata for core papers (Nov 2026)
finding: Citation counts show each paper's influence: March 1991 12505; Tushman and O'Reilly 1996 5057; He and Wong 2004 3972; Jansen 2006 3842; Gupta 2006 3421; Raisch and Birkinshaw 2008 2842; Raisch 2009 2315; Lubatkin 2006 2242; Cao 2009 1503; Junni 2013 907.
numbers: Counts as listed above.
limits: Counts differ between databases (IDEAS shows 777 for He and Wong).
agent_relevance: None for the agent; helps rank which papers to read next.
